title: Build a 304 SS Pressure Vessel
prompt: How would you make a 1 m diameter pressure vessel with a 3 mm wall out of 304 stainless?
solution: Sanity check first: P_yield = σ_y·t/r = 205 MPa × 3/500 ≈ 12 bar, so MEOP is about 8 bar at FS 1.5. Barrel: shear the 304L sheet (L-grade avoids weld sensitization) to a blank of about π × 1003 mm, roll it on a 3-roll bender, and TIG, plasma or laser weld the longitudinal seam with back purge so the root doesn't sugar. Domes: buy pressed or spun ellipsoidal heads, or hydroform them. Weld ports and bosses onto the domes before closing out. Fit up and weld the girth seams on a rotator for automation. Inspect: visual, PT on all welds, RT on the longitudinal and girth seams. Then hydro proof (about 1.5× MEOP) and a helium leak check.
keyPoints: Size check: ~12 bar to yield, ~8 bar MEOP
304L, roll the barrel, long seam
Purchased or spun or hydroformed domes
Back purge; automate girth welds on a rotator
PT and RT, hydro proof, leak test

title: Make the Accumulator Easier to Weld
prompt: You're given an existing accumulator design (a cylindrical pressure vessel with domes, ports and internal features). How would you change the design to make it easier to weld?
solution: Cut the weld count: use fewer pieces, formed domes and one-piece machined bosses. Prefer full-penetration butt joints over fillets and laps, and match thicknesses at the joint with machined tapers onto thicker weld lands. Move welds out of high-stress areas such as dome knuckles and discontinuities. Make every joint accessible to the torch or laser and to inspection (RT/UT), and leave room for back purge. Add self-fixturing features like step or joggle joints and locating lips, so fit-up gap is controlled without tooling. Make circumferential seams weldable on a rotator so they can be automated, avoid dissimilar metals, and plan the weld sequence to manage distortion.
keyPoints: Fewer welds; formed and machined parts
Butt joints, matched thicknesses, weld lands
Keep welds out of high-stress regions
Torch, inspection and purge access
Self-fixturing joints; automatable seams
Sequence for distortion

title: Manufacture 10,000 I-Beams
solution: Clarify first: what material, size, length, tolerance, load case, and over what timeframe (10k per year is about 40 a day). Standard steel sections: don't make them, buy hot-rolled sections from a mill and just cut, drill and coat them. Aluminum: extrusion, since the die cost amortizes easily over 10k parts. The flow is extrude, stretch-straighten, cut to length and heat treat to T6. Custom or large sections: welded plate girders on an automated line (plasma-cut the flanges and web, then submerged-arc or laser fillet welds) with distortion control. For any route, set the takt time, find the bottleneck station, design fixtures for repeatability, and use sampling inspection and SPC on the critical dimensions.
keyPoints: Clarify requirements and rate first
Buy standard hot-rolled sections
Aluminum: extrude, straighten, heat treat
Custom: automated welded plate girders
Takt time, bottleneck, fixtures, SPC

title: Trim Dome Petals at the Weld Station
prompt: A tank dome is built from formed petals (gores) that are welded together. Why might you cut each petal's final edge at the weld station, in the fixture, rather than trimming every petal to final size up front?
solution: Forming springback, cutting tolerance and fixture variation stack up. Petals pre-trimmed to nominal won't meet with the tight, uniform gap that welding needs, especially laser welding or FSW, where fit-up has to be within about a tenth of a millimeter. Trimming the mating edge in place, referenced to the fixture datums and the neighboring petal, absorbs all that upstream variation, so every seam gets the same gap. That gives consistent weld quality, less rework and scrap, and looser tolerances allowed at forming. The cost is a trim tool at the weld cell, and the cut edge needs to be clean (no burr or contamination) right before welding.
keyPoints: Tolerance stack: forming springback plus cutting plus fixture
Welding needs a tight, consistent gap
Cut-to-fit in the fixture absorbs upstream variation
Allows looser upstream tolerances; less scrap
Tradeoff: trim tooling at the weld cell, edge cleanliness

title: Roll Sheet into a Cylinder
prompt: You roll 3 mm sheet into a cylinder with a 1000 mm inside diameter. Explain the K-factor, then find the flat blank length (take K = 0.5, as for a large bend radius relative to thickness) and the approximate strain at the outer surface.
answer: ≈ 3151 mm blank; ≈ +0.3% strain on OD (−0.3% on ID)
solution:
K-factor = neutral-axis offset from the inside surface divided by thickness. The neutral axis keeps its length. Material outside it stretches and inside it compresses. K ≈ 0.5 for large R/t, and it falls to about 0.3–0.45 for tight bends as the axis shifts inward.
Blank length = π·(ID + 2Kt) = π × (1000 + 3) ≈ 3151 mm.
Outer-fiber strain ≈ (t/2)/R_n = 1.5/501.5 ≈ 0.30% tension, with equal compression on the ID. That's tiny, so a 1 m roll is well within elastic-plastic limits, but springback matters.

keyPoints: Failure starts at weld ends, not mid-weld
Gusset tip on tube: shear lag and stiffness hard spot
Outer toe on flange: peel from flange bending
Uncoped corner where welds intersect
Fixes: soft toe, wrapped ends, cope, ground toes
title: Gusset Weld Pull-Off Failure
prompt: A flange is welded to the end of a tube and reinforced with triangular gussets welded to both the tube and the flange. If the flange is pulled axially off the tube, where on the gusset welds would you expect failure to start, and why?
solution: At the weld terminations, not mid-length. The most likely spot is the gusset tip on the tube, where the gusset ends abruptly. Load funnels into the end of the weld (shear lag), and the sudden stiffness change plus the weld start/stop defects make a hot spot. The second candidate is the gusset's outer toe on the flange, where flange bending peels the weld. If the gusset corner wasn't coped, the intersection with the tube-to-flange weld is also a crack starter. Fixes: taper or radius the gusset tip (a soft toe), wrap the weld ends, cope the corner, and grind the toes smooth.

keyPoints: Low shear flow: continuous weld unnecessary
Less heat: less distortion and HAZ softening
Faster, lighter, less filler
Cons: stitch ends are fatigue starters
Cons: crevices trap contamination; lower stiffness
title: Stitch Welding Tank Stiffeners
prompt: Why would you use stitch (intermittent) welds instead of continuous welds to attach stiffeners to a propellant tank wall? What are the downsides?
solution: Stiffener-to-skin joints carry low shear flow, so a continuous weld is mostly unnecessary. Stitching cuts heat input, which means less distortion and residual stress in the thin skin, and less HAZ softening of the pressure wall (a big deal for aluminum alloys). It also saves weld time, filler and mass. Downsides: every stitch end is a stress concentration and a fatigue initiation site, the gaps between stitches are crevices that trap moisture and contamination (corrosion, cleanliness for LOX service), and the stiffener is less effective in buckling than with a continuous joint.

title: Post-Processing a Printed 17-4 Injector
prompt: Walk through the post-processing steps for a freshly printed (LPBF) 17-4 PH stainless injector, including heat treatment.
solution: On the build plate: depowder first, especially the internal manifolds and orifices, because trapped powder sinters during heat treatment. Then stress relieve on the plate so it doesn't distort, and wire-EDM it off. Remove supports. HIP if fatigue or porosity matters. Solution anneal at about 1040 °C (Condition A) and cool fast. Printed 17-4 can retain austenite, so add a cryo step if needed to finish the martensite transformation. Age: H900 for strength, or H1025/H1150 for toughness and SCC resistance. Then machine sealing faces and threads, ream or EDM the orifices to final size, and smooth the internal passages (abrasive flow or chemical polish). Finish with oxygen cleaning, CT scan for blockages and porosity, CMM, proof and leak tests, and a waterflow test to verify flow and patternation.
